analysis.one_liner: Sets federal minimum wages regionally, scaled to local living costs and rising with average wages.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in May 2025 with two cosponsors, was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee, which has taken no action on it.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would replace the flat $7.25 federal minimum wage with a wage that varies by metro area and rural region, pegged to a share of the national average hourly wage and adjusted up or down for local living costs. The share starts at 40% of the national average wage and steps up to 50% within two years, then keeps pace with wage growth. It would also raise the cash wage for tipped workers to 30% of their area's minimum and raise the youth subminimum wage from $4.25 to two-thirds of the area's minimum.
analysis.who_benefits: Millions of workers now paid at or near the $7.25 federal floor, especially in high-cost metro areas where the regional formula would produce the biggest raises. Tipped workers gain because the cash wage employers must pay before tips counts would rise well above today's $2.13. Workers under 25 hired into the subminimum track would see that rate jump from $4.25 to a share of the local minimum.

how_it_helps.text: Replaces the single $7.25 federal minimum with a wage set separately for each metropolitan area and each state's rural counties, so wages reflect what things cost where people work.
Sets the regional wage at 40% of the national average hourly wage for private non-supervisory workers, rising to 45% within a year and 50% within two years, then never lower than that going forward.
Adjusts the regional wage up or down for local price levels, from 87.5% of the formula in the cheapest areas to 115% in the most expensive ones.
Raises the minimum cash wage for tipped employees from the frozen $2.13 to 30% of the area's minimum wage.
Raises the youth subminimum wage from $4.25 an hour to two-thirds of the area's minimum wage.

analysis.who_pays: Businesses with large low-wage workforces — restaurants, fast food, retail, hospitality, and agriculture — would bear higher payroll costs, concentrated in the roughly 20-plus states that still use the $7.25 federal floor. Tipped-restaurant employers would see the sharpest change, since their required cash wage would more than triple. Consumers could pay somewhat more at those businesses.

drawbacks.text: The regional formula leaves minimums far apart: in low-cost areas the starting wage would be roughly $10–$11 an hour (40% of a ~$30 national average times the 87.5% adjustment), a much smaller raise than a single national increase would give, and still below the minimums some states already have.

The bill widens the youth subminimum track: it raises the subminimum rate but extends eligibility from workers under 20 to workers 24 and younger, letting more adults legally be paid below the full minimum.
It keeps a tipped subminimum in place rather than eliminating the tip credit — tipped workers would still depend on tips to reach full pay.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A real raise for workers in the many states stuck at $7.25, especially in high-cost cities, and a meaningful bump for tipped and youth workers. The trade-offs are deliberate design choices: regional adjustment means smaller raises in cheaper areas, the youth subminimum now covers workers up to 24, and the tipped subminimum survives. Compared with a flat national increase, it spreads the cost more evenly across regions but gives less to workers in low-cost states.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Education and Workforce Committee, which has not scheduled any action on it, so it is waiting with no path forward so far.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 15, 2025, by Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick with Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce.
It has two cosponsors, one Democrat and one Republican.
No further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — appears in the bill's action history.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers still paying the $7.25 federal minimum, and the tipped-restaurant industry in particular, are better off because nothing has moved: no wage increase has been scheduled for consideration. Low-wage workers in those states have gained nothing.

against.what_they_did: Has not brought a minimum wage increase to the floor; the bill has sat in committee since May 2025.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship is bipartisan — a Republican sponsor with a Democratic cosponsor and one more cosponsor from the other party — but with only three members involved, no party split has really been tested.

industries.note: The bill would more than triple the cash wage they must pay tipped staff, from $2.13 to 30% of the area minimum. Since the industry profits by keeping that cash wage near zero, its interest runs against the workers' raise. Nothing has happened yet because the bill is stalled.

industries.industry: Low-wage employers generally (retail, fast food, agriculture, care work)
industries.note: Employers in the states using the $7.25 federal floor would face the largest payroll increases. Their interest in keeping the current floor is the flip side of workers' gain.
The 115% regional adjustment would push minimums in expensive metros well above $15, but many large employers there already pay at or above those levels, so the added cost falls unevenly.

analysis.trajectory: With two cosponsors and no committee action more than a year into the two-year session, the bill has the typical profile of a bill that will not advance: most bills referred to committee in this position never get a hearing or vote. Advancing would require the committee chair to schedule a markup and House leadership to prioritize a wage increase, neither of which has shown signs of happening.
